In the badminton academy canteen, Naveen had heard all of his friend Arohi's stories: the state camp invite, the top coach who had "begged" to train her, the scholarship from abroad. He had repeated some of them to his cousin with real pride.
On Thursday the district selection list went up on the academy notice board. Arohi's name wasn't on it. There was no state camp either. When Naveen asked the coach, the coach said gently, "She's a good player. There was never an invitation."
Naveen sat on the bench for a long time, red-faced, thinking of his cousin. Later, when Arohi mentioned a new sponsor, he just nodded. He didn't believe her, and he realised he no longer believed the true things she said either.

qa.q: Where did the district selection list go up?
qa.a: The list went up on the academy notice board.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling on the bench, and why?
qa.a: He felt foolish and embarrassed, because he had proudly repeated Arohi's stories to his cousin.

qa.q: What could Naveen do to keep the friendship while being careful about what he believes?
qa.a: He could tell Arohi calmly that the stretched stories hurt his trust, and keep valuing what he can see for himself, like her play.

qa.q: How might Arohi's habit affect how others see her real achievements?
qa.a: Even her real skill may be doubted, because Naveen now disbelieves the true things she says as well.

grounding: A teenager who believed a friend's grand stories learns they were stretched, feels foolish, and finds that everything she says now counts for less.

Yogesh,
I'm writing this instead of saying it, because you'd laugh it off like you always do.
On Saturday I brought four people to the college gate because you said your "contact" could get us backstage at the fest. We stood outside for two hours. You stopped answering your phone. Later you said the contact "had a family emergency".
It's not only Saturday. The foreign trip that turned into a cousin's wedding two towns away. The "national-level" quiz that was a school round. I believed all of it, and I told people, and now they look at me like I'm the gullible one.
I still want to be friends. But I've started halving everything you say, and I hate doing that. Can we just keep it real?
Imran

qa.a: They stood outside for two hours.

qa.q: How does Imran feel about having believed Yogesh, and what shows it?
qa.a: Imran feels foolish and hurt; people now see Imran as the gullible one, and Imran has started halving everything Yogesh says.

qa.q: Which part of the letter is a wise step, and why?
qa.a: Imran names specific examples and still says the friendship matters, which makes it easier for Yogesh to listen instead of laughing it off.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Yogesh may feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but seeing the real cost to Imran could push Yogesh towards being more honest.

grounding: A teenager writes to a friend whose inflated claims left the writer embarrassed and less trusting of everything the friend says.

First week of June. Siddharth told Vinita his cousin was a coach at the state cricket academy and could get them both into the summer camp, free. Vinita skipped signing up for the school camp and told her parents she was going somewhere much better.
Mid-June. Siddharth said the cousin was busy but it was "confirmed." He also mentioned he'd met a famous player at a wedding. Vinita believed that too.
End of June. Vinita went with her father to the academy to ask about dates. The man at the desk had never heard of any cousin. The camp had started a week ago.
In the car, Vinita stared out the window. She felt stupid for believing him, and embarrassed in front of her father. Worse, she started going back through everything Siddharth had ever told her, and she wasn't sure which parts had been true.

qa.a: He said his cousin was a coach at the state cricket academy.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel in the car?
qa.a: Vinita felt foolish and embarrassed, and she began to distrust everything Siddharth had ever told her.

qa.q: What could Vinita do next time a friend makes a big promise?
qa.a: She could check it directly, like asking the academy or a teacher, before giving up other plans.

qa.q: What would change for Siddharth after this?
qa.a: His other stories would carry less weight, because Vinita now doubts even the ordinary things he says.

Deepak, you asked why I check everything twice. Let me, your old Francis Uncle, tell you about Nicky, my best friend when I was sixteen in Goa.
Nicky had stories. His father had sailed to Brazil. His uncle knew a film director. He had once swum across the whole bay. And I believed every word, because he told them so well.
One summer he said he could get us jobs on a fishing trawler for the holidays. I told my mother I'd be away two weeks. I packed a bag. On the morning we were to leave, Nicky didn't come. Later I learned there was no trawler, and his father had never left Goa.
I wasn't angry at first. I just felt foolish, standing with my bag at the jetty. Afterwards, even when Nicky told me true things, I couldn't believe them. I kept thinking: which part is stretched?

qa.q: Where was Francis waiting with his bag?
qa.a: He was standing with his bag at the jetty.

qa.q: How did young Francis feel at the jetty?
qa.a: He felt foolish and let down, realising he had believed and planned around Nicky's stretched story.

qa.q: At what turning point could young Francis have protected himself?
qa.a: Before telling his mother and packing, he could have checked with the trawler owners or an adult whether the jobs were real.

qa.q: How might Nicky's stories have been affected after that summer?
qa.a: Even Nicky's true stories lost their value, because Francis could no longer tell which parts were stretched.

grounding: An uncle recalls believing a friend's grand stories as a teenager, feeling foolish when they proved stretched, and trusting him less afterwards.

The inter-house relay was in twenty minutes, the coach was stuck in traffic, and Leela, as house captain, had to fill the last swimming spot herself.
"Take Mahima," she told the vice-captain. "She's a state-level swimmer. She told me so herself, loads of times."
Mahima's face went pale when she heard. "Leela, I… it was a small club thing. Years ago."
"You said state level. You said you won medals."
"I said I swam at a state meet. Once. I came last."
The whistle blew for warm-up. There was no one else to ask. Leela felt her face burn. She had repeated Mahima's stories to the whole house.
Mahima swam her lap slowly but finished. Their house came fourth.
Afterwards, Leela sat on the steps, quiet. Mahima came and sat nearby. Leela didn't know what to say. She wasn't sure she would believe Mahima's next story at all.

qa.q: Where did Mahima say she came at the state meet?
qa.a: She said she came last.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she learned the truth?
qa.a: Leela felt embarrassed and foolish, her face burning, because she had repeated Mahima's stories to the whole house.

qa.q: What could Leela do next time before relying on a claim like that?
qa.a: She could ask a simple checking question or see the person swim before choosing them, instead of trusting repeated stories.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima when Leela names her as a state-level swimmer?
qa.a: Mahima feels panicked and exposed, because her stretched stories are suddenly tested in front of everyone.

grounding: It shows a teenager who trusted a friend's inflated claims discovering the stretch under pressure, and feeling foolish and less trusting.

For a whole term, Usha believed everything Ganga said. Ganga's cousin worked "with" a famous film director. Ganga had "nearly" been picked for the state cricket team. Ganga had been to London "last summer".
Then, at a birthday party in their Pune colony, Ganga's mother laughed while serving cake. "London? Ganga's never been further than Nashik!" The cousin, it turned out, drove a van for a catering company that sometimes worked on film sets.
Usha felt her face go hot. She had repeated the London story to her own cousins.
Walking home, she went through everything Ganga had ever told her. Which bits were true? The cricket? The time Ganga said Usha's drawing was "the best in the class"?
The next week, when Ganga talked about a new phone that was coming, Usha just said, "Nice," and didn't believe a word.

qa.q: How far had Ganga really travelled?
qa.a: Ganga's never been further than Nashik.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after Ganga's mother's comment?
qa.a: Usha felt foolish and embarrassed, face hot, having repeated the London story to her own cousins.

qa.q: What could Usha do instead of silently doubting everything?
qa.a: Tell Ganga honestly how the stretched stories felt, so the friendship has a chance to become real again.

qa.q: What has Ganga lost through the exaggerations?
qa.a: Even true things Ganga says, like praise for Usha's drawing, are now doubted, so Ganga's words have lost their value.
